newsitem.title: ITALY: Berisha does deal, southern Albania rebels dig in.
newsitem.headline: Berisha does deal, southern Albania rebels dig in.

text.p: Albania's embattled President Sali Berisha agreed on Thursday to suspend military action against armed insurgents in the south as international pressure mounted to avert a bloodbath.
The decision was announced in a statement in Tirana after Berisha met opposition leaders for more than five hours.
It came on the eve of a visit to the Balkan state by Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo with a "clear message" from the European Union to reach a political solution to the crisis.

The statement said participants had agreed that offensive action should be halted for 48 hours from 6 a.m. (0500 GMT) on Friday. Rebels were to start surrendering weapons at the same time and would be amnestied if they had not committed crimes.
Signatories "supported the restoration of constitutional order and guaranteeing public order throughout the country".

It was the first substantial political breakthrough since protesters angered by the loss of life savings in shady pyramid investment schemes seized weapons from police and army stores and took control of several southern towns at the weekend.

Parliament, dominated by Berisha's ruling Democratic Party, responded by declaring a state of emergency but the push to restore authority appeared to falter on Thursday as rebels dug in against any attempt to crush their uprising.

Reuter reporters in the troubled south said anti-Berisha army officers in the town of Tepelene had gone over to the rebel side while in Sarande, on the Adriatic coast, heavily-armed insurgents held two suspected police agents hostage.

One man was to be sent before a "people's court" while the second man's fate was unknown. He was tied to a telephone pole and kicked in the face on Wednesday before being dragged before a mob in the main square to "confess".

The official news agency ATA said the death toll in Vlore, epicentre of the unrest, had risen to 25 since Friday and an Italian nun reported from the port that armed men had looted the hospital. She appealed for swift humanitarian assistance.

"They have taken everything away and we don't know how we are going to treat the burns and gunshot wounds," the Italian news agency ANSA quoted the nun, who was not identified, as saying by telephone.

Berisha's agreement to hold fire was accompanied by an undertaking to seek consensus on a replacement for his deeply unpopular outgoing Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi, whose resignation was announced last Saturday.
But a top Social Democrat, Paskal Milo, said the talks had achieved nothing as Berisha had yet to agree to the principle of a coalition government.
In Rome, The Netherlands' Van Mierlo said he would ask Berisha and the opposition during talks in Tirana on Friday to achieve a political solution to the unrest.

"We should do this in the interest of Albania (but) it's in the interest of Europe also that we do everything to get a political solution in Albania," Van Mierlo, whose country holds the EU presidency, said before leaving for talks in Athens on his way to Tirana.
The Van Mierlo mission will be the highest-level visit to Tirana since the uprising erupted.

A Council of Europe delegation was also in Tirana on Thursday and former Austrian chancellor Franz Vranitzky, named by Europe's OSCE security forum to lead a mission, said Berisha had agreed his visit should go ahead as soon as possible.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, who met Van Mierlo, said Berisha had promised not to use force to quell the unrest.
Dini said Berisha and the opposition should work for a government of national reconciliation to lead Albania, Europe's poorest state, to peace and an early general election.
"The only solution is a political settlement. It is not through the revolt, it is not through use of the military...that the Albanian problem will be resolved," Dini said.

The insurrection has rung alarm bells in Albania's neighbour Greece and in Italy, where impoverished illegal emigrants have headed in their tens of thousands since 45 years of iron-fisted Stalinist rule crumbled in 1991.
Greek Deputy Foreign Minister Georges Papandreou warned that trouble there could spread through the Balkans.
"We Greeks want the crisis contained within the borders of Albania and not to spread to the ex-Yugoslav Macedonia, to Bulgaria or to Kosovo," he told the French newspaper Le Monde.
The United States and Italy said on Thursday that they were drafting contingency plans to evacuate their nationals from Albania if the unrest worsened.
Some 1,600 Americans live in Albania. Italy airlifted 35 foreigners out of Vlore on Monday but a considerable number of Italians still live in Tirana and other towns.
